notes: Coder A's per-unit 'why' fields were written after coding (disclosed in A's notes) and were ignored; every disagreement was settled by re-reading the saved source text, and no unit rationales were added to v2/inst (validated with --no-why). Units were aligned by anchor/sentence overlap, with these hand fixes: in the Grainger guidance page the anchor 'will be considered academic dishonesty and a violation of the University of Illinois Student Code' occurs twice, so the aligner mis-paired A19 with B3; re-paired as A3-B3 (Restricted template) and A19-B19 (Use When Instructed template, final anchor taken from B19 so it is unique). Also paired adjacent-sentence units that state the same rule: Grainger template 'You may use generative AI in ___ for the following' / 'Add acceptable uses here' (and the MAY NOT pair), CS 124 AI page 'inspired and guided by our own usage' / 'These experiences inform how we teach', CS 124 AI cost sentences ('endeavor to keep the cost reasonable' / 'an amount we consider appropriate'), CS 124 syllabus 'Only work on your CS 124 project counts' / 'conversations unrelated to your project do not count' (resolved must-not, B's anchor, because the passage adds 'do not belong in your project folder'), and CS 128 prescribed prompt header ('Some assignments specify...' / 'Where an assignment specifies such a requirement, you must follow it'). STANCE: agreed on 9 of 10 documents. Grainger 'Using AI' A permit / B delegates -> permit: the page itself sorts uses into appropriate ('augment human thinking') and inappropriate ('replace human thinking') and never hands the decision to instructors. PATTERN 1, policy_type (46 matched disagreements; about a fifth are the instructor-use NEW type below). CITL and Grainger 'Using AI' instructor uses (draft syllabi/rubrics/quiz items, example datasets, format conversion, recommendation letters, AI email replies): A used P48/P17/P18/P47, B used NEW:Instructor use of AI for teaching work; resolved to the NEW type (P48 is review/disclosure of AI-made materials, P17 a sanctioned tool for students, neither says what instructors may use AI for). Translation in general stays P18/all; translating recommendation letters goes to the NEW type. Other type calls: Grainger 'informed when, where, and how these tools are permitted' -> P09 (B); 'provided with examples of how to cite' -> P25 (A, citation format, as in GT); CS 411 'without substantive assistance from others, including automated tools' -> P45 (A); CS 411 'strictly prohibited for homework' -> P01 (A). CS 124 AI page: 'introduces students to ... coding agents' and 'conversational programming requires creativity' -> P44 (B); instructor 'collaborating with Claude Code on courseware' -> P47 (describes own use to students); scaffold steps (create repository, workshops) and 'work with AI coding agents, not human partners' -> P35 (B); future prompting challenges on quizzes -> P35 (assessment change, not a policy review); 'We'll teach you how to [validate]' -> P44 to match the agreed parallel unit; AI concepts on quizzes -> P44; tutors helping understand AI code -> P30. CS 124 syllabus: 'design and build ... using AI coding agents' -> P35 (matches the AI page); 'an agent writing your code is the assignment there' -> P04; 'It is yours, genuinely your own creative work' (publish anywhere) -> P52; 'asking questions is fine, getting answers is not' -> must-not P19 (it states where the line falls; the permitted half is coded separately); unattended-agent sentence -> P07. CS 128: 'AI tools may be used only in accordance with the AI Policy' -> may/P02; 'AI may support your process' -> P02 (specific supports are coded separately); 'Here's the assignment prompt. Write the solution.' -> P19 (the course allows pasting the prompt to understand it); 'hands the problem to the AI fails this condition' and 'understanding afterward does not repair' -> P32 (they elaborate the agreed 'you must solve the problem' condition); 'Iteratively prompting until tests pass' -> P30 (listed under the explain-every-line condition); reflection form contents and attestation -> P26. CS 225 'teaches you far less than you realize' -> P43. IS 445 'we want to see how you problem-solve' -> P32; 'must not constitute the primary source of content or answers' -> P19; 'validation plan' -> P31. PATTERN 2, actor on statements addressed to students. A often coded grading and procedure sentences as instructor/ta-staff, B as student; B often coded facts as all. Following the UC Irvine rule (actor = who the passage addresses), CS 124 syllabus sentences written to 'you' (graded on hours, hours measured from Claude Code sessions, prompt time accounting, 'two different sets of rules', 'is this work actually yours?', other courses' AI policies, AI's real costs) -> student. Statements with no addressee ('Employers expect graduates...', 'the valuable human contribution is formulating the idea', 'The two halves of the course now have their own rules', Grainger 'Using AI' paper-summary examples) -> all. 'Our staff' / 'we select' / 'our assessment' (CS 128 code interviews, ECE 220) -> instructor (course staff as a body; ta-staff kept for rules aimed at TAs or graders). AI course assistant use and 'We recommend Claude' -> student. PATTERN 3, modality. (a) Consequence and descriptive statements: Grainger 'considered plagiarism and will not be tolerated', CS 124 scaffold descriptions and syllabus arc labels ('Build a throwaway prototype...', 'Build your app with Claude Code'), '24 measured hours ... to earn the 18 points', 'should expect to purchase', rationale sentences ('it is still critical that users develop ... classical programming', 'the project itself needs to be designed around AI collaboration', 'being shown the answer is not as useful'), and Grainger fact sentences under 'Inappropriate Usage Examples' (email replies, job applications) -> informs, as in GT. (b) Staff procedural commitments -> must: 'we will continue to monitor', 'we select some students' (code interviews), 'Your project code is still checked', 'Evidence ... will initiate academic integrity proceedings', ECE 391 'processed through the FAIR system'; this matches the agreed 'We will run automated checks' unit. (c) Literal wording wins otherwise: 'should be limited to debugging', 'Such usage should be restricted', 'should not be used in their submissions', 'not meant to be used in place of', 'avoiding uploading student work', 'we expect it to' -> should/should-not; IS 445 imperative 'Cross-reference...' -> must (GT imperative rule); CITL 'Faculty can model curiosity' -> may; 'CITL staff can help you' -> informs; CS 225 'current opinion of the course staff is that AI tools should be taught after...' -> informs (a stated view). PATTERN 4, phase. Definitions of misconduct in the CS 124 project list (cheating, plagiarism, fabrication, facilitation, interference) -> during-work (A): they name forbidden conduct while working; sanctions and proceedings stay when-misuse. CS 128 code-interview rules -> during-assessment. P10 'ask if unsure' units -> course-start (as in GT/UCI). Course-design rationales on the CS 124 pages ('the old model ... is broken', 'tension between precise specifications') -> before-course; scope and disclosure notes ('only teaches AI-supported programming on the project', 'Claude reviewed the document', IS 445 'policy ... generated by ChatGPT', CITL closing invitation) -> general. PATTERN 5, merged vs split units and only-one-coder units. Kept B's splits where one sentence holds two rules (CS 128 specstory recommendation vs the save-it-yourself fallback; 'understanding afterward does not repair' vs the P41 rationale) and A's splits likewise (CS 225 'code is checked for plagiarism' vs 'same tools produce similar solutions'; 'assignments are structured to teach you'; Grainger 'Using AI' translation in general vs translating recommendation letters; CS 124 5-hour weekly cap vs the 24-hour requirement; CS 128 'you may work from an AI tool's suggestions' for tests). Kept only-A: the 'Using AI' overview sentences (proofreading, materials, datasets, translation, format conversion, tutoring, limitations), which are not exact repeats; CITL intro rationale sentences, 'impress these standards on their students', 'Queries may produce incorrect authors and citations'; CS 128 appropriate-prompt examples (the inappropriate ones were coded by both), 'earn full marks without ever using an AI tool'; CS 124 hardware/laptop-loan/contact-instructor access units tied to the Claude app, Code-tab paid plan, scaffold and design rationales, cost, 'That's expected when doing conversational programming', 'Most courses define academic integrity by authorship' (retyped P29 to match its agreed neighbour), 'Hours are measured by software', forum check of hours; ECE 391 IDE ban sentence and 'responsible for all work your group turns in'. Dropped only-A: CS 225 'Unless directly stated in an assignment' (first clause of the agreed P01 sentence, whose final text keeps the condition); Grainger Restricted 'will find their place in our workforces' (concessive clause of the agreed P41 sentence) and the Use When Instructed must-not, which only restates as a prohibition what the sentence states as a consequence; CITL College of Law link (navigation); CS 124 'never accepting done without looking' (a lesson-topic clause inside the agreed lesson unit) and 'come away understanding what you made' (merged into the agreed P30 unit with B's anchor and text); CS 124 grade breakdown and lesson-time sentence (no AI content); 'Bribes, favors, and threats' and CS 128 'Course staff are not responsible for warning you' (generic integrity rules with no AI content, which both coders otherwise skipped). Kept only-B: Grainger 'there are times when generative AI may be useful' (resolved informs, P04) and 'During our class, we may use AI tools'; 'Using AI' prompting tip and the purpose footer (coded on the guidance page by both); CS 124 'preparing students today for the programming of today', 'tremendously exciting', 'Other courses will take different approaches', 'We want you to learn how to use AI effectively', scaffold/arc units, 'AI policies vary across contexts' (actor student), 'The fact that you can use AI does not mean you should'; CS 128 save-it-yourself fallback and P41 rationale; ECE 391 work-products and team-responsibility rules; IS 445 purpose-of-assignments rationale and the disclosed prompts. Dropped only-B: the Kailash Nadh quotation on the CS 124 AI page (an outside author's quote, like the CITL testimonials both coders skipped), 'Using AI' manuscript peer review (research, outside teaching and learning; A's notes excluded it too), CS 128 'We want you exposed to ... frontier models' (first clause of the sentence coded as one unit, with A's text kept), ECE 391 'Any code you did not write yourself' (a list item with no AI mention; the AI-tools item is its own unit). NEW TYPES. (1) Coder B's NEW:Instructor use of AI for teaching work: KEPT (14 units: CITL 5, Grainger 'Using AI' 9). No existing type says what instructors may or should not use AI for in their own teaching work; P46 (grading), P47 (disclosing own use to students) and P48 (reviewing/disclosing AI-made materials) each cover a different rule. The definition was narrowed to teaching work, dropping manuscript peer review (the only peer-review unit was dropped as out of scope). (2) Coder A's NEW:Prescribed AI interaction protocol (CS 128 required prompt header): MERGED into P35. An assignment-specified opening prompt or interaction protocol is an assignment structured around AI, which is what P35 covers (B coded it P35). It occurs once in the dry run. Suggest adding 'required prompt headers or interaction protocols' to P35's examples. (3) Coder A's NEW:Decline to police AI use (ECE 220 'Our staff will not actively police your use of generative AI'; B had P39): KEPT. The sentence states a non-enforcement posture, with consequences left to AI-free exams. P39 is about detectors being unreliable or not used as proof while enforcement continues by other means, and P03 is the separately coded discouragement. Actor set to instructor.
